https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/07/orba.text: Menü Kereső MCC-s libsi pénzégetés és permanens zsebhokizás – Huth Gergely szekunder szégyent érez Orbán Balázstól Belföld frissítve Huth Gergely Tusványoson – Fotó: Hevesi-Szabó Lujza / Telex Patakfalvi Dóra Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Úgy tűnik, a korábbi kormányoldal talált legalább egy felelőst a Fidesz választási bukásáért. Orbán Balázs előbb a Hír TV -ben élt át váratlanul izzasztó pillanatokat, majd Huth Gergely is arról posztolt: az MCC vezetőjének működése szekunder szégyenérzetet váltott ki a teljes jobboldalon, és a „kivagyi új elit” vezéralakjának nevezte. Huth azt írta: „Az MCC-s libsi pénzégetés, az Oscar-gálákat idéző nyálas tobzódások, a fehér kesztyűs fogadásokon előadott, kínosan üres hablatyolások, a határon túli nemzettársaink mételyezése (például a megalázó MCC-s román tanfolyamokkal), a huszárvágások helyett produkált permanens zsebhokizás mind-mind a közelgő összeomlás előjelei voltak.” Orbán Balázst a Hír TV Monitor című műsorában Ferkó Dániel többek között arról kérdezte, fideszes képviselőként miért jár be olyan keveset a magyar Országgyűlésbe, és hogyan képzeli a munkáját az Európai Parlamentben. A Fidesz kampányát vezénylő Orbán Balázs erre azt válaszolta, leginkább a pártjuk nemzetközi koalíciójának megszervezésén dolgozik, és az a céljuk, hogy a Fidesz és a Patrióták ellenzékből is az európai politika meghatározó szereplője legyen, a szervezési munka pedig sok energiát igényel. De Ferkó nem adta ilyen könnyen, és azzal szembesítette Orbánt, hogy lényegében átmentette magát, miközben nyilvánvaló volt, hogy nem fogja kitölteni a magyar parlamenti mandátumát, és ezekre a hónapokra is kap fizetést. A politikus azzal vágta ki magát, hogy Szekeres Pál a tavaszi–nyári ülésszakot szerette volna lezárni, és ha Orbán Balázs lemond, a helye betöltetlen marad. A műsorvezető ezután ráfordult az MCC ügyére, és a Telex cikkét idézte, amelyben egy, a kötelékükbe tartozó tanár azt nyilatkozta: az ott tanuló diákok többsége a Tisza Pártra szavazott. „Mit gondol, ezek után megérte milliárdokat feccölni az MCC-be?” – kérdezte Ferkó. Orbán szerint az MCC tehetséggondozásról és nem pártképzésről szólt, vagyis megérte. Ők csak egy anti-Soros megközelítésű think tanket működtettek, mondta Orbán, a műsorvezető szerint viszont ez is aligha jött be, hiszen liberális lett a diákjaik többsége. Ezt a beszélgetést osztotta meg a Pesti Srácok egykori főszerkesztője, Huth Gergely az oldalán , aki azt írta: „Ferkó Dániel zseniálisan falhoz szorította Orbán Balázst, a bukás legfőbb felelősét”, aki rávilágított, hogy „a zsíros EP-mandátummal még meg is jutalmazzák”, és Huth szerint Orbán a műsorvezetőnek adott válaszai „nem voltak túl meggyőzőek”. Majd úgy folytatta, Orbán Viktor ötször hozott diadalt a nemzeti jobboldalnak, és szerinte „a Napnál is világosabb, hogy a vétkeseket az utolsó négy évben a felszínre sodródott aktorokban kell keresni”. Majd azt írta: „Tehát a magyarok számára idegen és taszító, kivagyi új elit köreiben, melynek vezéralakja éppen Orbán Balázs volt. Neki gyakorlatilag semmi sem sikerült, működése szekunder szégyenérzetet váltott ki a teljes jobboldalon.” Huth végül Orbán Balázst „amúgy kellemes figurának és kiváló társasági embernek nevezte”, de szerinte „a tengernyi bűn nem járhat jutalommal”. https://www.politico.eu/article/how-did-.text: Ursula von der Leyen used her set piece speech last year to declare Europe's "independence moment." Twelve months later, the European Commission president's record shows the EU's independence still very much depends on its national capitals. One year after her last State of the Union address, von der Leyen has delivered most clearly where the Commission could act largely on its own: writing laws and funding initiatives on core topics like tech, trade and social policy. She struggled most where success required member countries to agree, surrender more control to Brussels or build genuinely new European capabilities — particularly on defense. Advertisement Advertisement “The issue of defense plays a completely different role in Europe than it did just two years ago,” said Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, the liberal chair of the European Parliament’s security and defense committee, pointing to a series of “very valuable programs” launched over the past year. But, she added, “all efforts are reaching their limits, because national self-interest continues to play a major role.” That tension runs through POLITICO’s assessment of the promises in von der Leyen’s last State of the Union address. Of more than 40 announcements — broadly defined as commitments that could plausibly be turned into action — roughly 15 politically significant commitments stand out. Von der Leyen framed promises including a drone wall, an India trade deal and an affordable housing plan as part of a wider push for European sovereignty. Where von der Leyen struggled was with the promises that were supposed to change what Europe actually is and create its supposed “independence moment.” Those were the promises that made last year’s speech feel bigger than a normal Commission work program. And those are the areas where the gap between ambition and reality remains widest. Advertisement Advertisement Clearest misses Few lines from last year’s speech were more memorable than von der Leyen’s promise to build a “drone wall.” The idea was presented as a jointly developed, real-time European capability to detect and counter aerial threats. The concept quickly ran into political resistance at the informal European Council meeting in Copenhagen on Oct. 1, and evolved into a broader counter-drone action plan. The integrated European capability as originally advertised did not materialize within the year. The second major miss was von der Leyen’s plan to use immobilized Russian assets to fund a reparations loan for Ukraine. “The issue of defense plays a completely different role in Europe than it did just two years ago,” said Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann. | I-Hwa Cheng/AFP via Getty Images It was one of the most creative financing ideas put forward by the EU. It also ran straight into legal and political problems. By December 2025, EU leaders were still asking officials to keep working on the technical details. In the end, Europe agreed on a €90 billion Ukraine loan with more conventional financing through EU borrowing and backed by the EU budget. Then there was the European Defence Semester. The name itself was ambitious: regular EU-level scrutiny and coordination of national defense efforts, echoing the European Semester used to grade capitals' economic policy. Advertisement Advertisement That concept never really took shape. What emerged was closer to an annual defense-readiness reporting and coordination exercise, leaving member countries with considerably more control. Clearest success The performance improves once you move away from the Europe von der Leyen described as "in a fight" and toward its traditional peace project ambitions — things the Commission can directly propose or organize. Her trade goals represent a virtual clean sweep. The Commission followed through on its diversification agenda, including negotiations with India — the deal arrived slightly later than von der Leyen had promised, but the substance was delivered. The Mercosur trade deal with Latin America also provisionally entered into force, after over a quarter century of negotiations. Social policy was also one of the strongest areas. The Commission produced an affordable housing plan in December 2025, followed by an act this week. In May, von der Leyen announced an anti-poverty strategy. Industrial and technology policy also moved forward in line with what she promised, including initiatives covering batteries, the cloud, AI and energy grids. The announced Industrial Accelerator Act and its “Made in Europe” provisions, which would seek to channel public procurement to drive green industrial development, landed in March and is now being reviewed by the Council and Parliament. Advertisement Advertisement Notably, much of the work came from commissioners belonging to political families other than von der Leyen’s own European People’s Party, including socialist and liberal members of the College. Foreign policy also produced some clear results in line with the commitments of last year’s State of the Union speech. The EU held the promised high-level meeting on abducted Ukrainian children in May, and another sanctions package against Russia was adopted in October 2025. Von der Leyen explicitly cited Australia’s approach to social-media restrictions for children. | George Chan/Getty Images The Commission also delivered the announced European Democracy Shield , while the European Centre for Democratic Resilience began operating in February 2026. The plans in the initiative may have seriously disappointed lawmakers , but the body is indeed working on three programs led by France, Poland and Sweden to improve the EU's defense against misinformation. Even one of the smaller promises came through: the European firefighting hub in Cyprus was launched in time for the 2026 fire season. The awkward middle Some promises sit somewhere between success and failure, with the fairest label being “in progress.” Social-media restrictions for children are one example. Von der Leyen promised that experts would examine possible European measures and explicitly cited Australia’s approach, which bans under-16s from holding social media accounts and puts the responsibility for enforcing the age limit on the platforms themselves. Advertisement Advertisement That process took place, and the issue has moved considerably further up the EU political agenda. But the decisive step — an EU-wide restriction regime — remains unfinished. The same applies to parts of her Israel policy shift. Von der Leyen used last year’s speech to promise sanctions against extremist ministers and violent settlers, a partial suspension of EU-Israel trade preferences and a donor mechanism for Palestine. Some of that agenda moved. Further sanctions were adopted against extremist settlers, and the Palestine donor structure became real, including the €883.6 million Team Gaza Initiative to coordinate funding for Gaza’s early recovery, launched in July. But the most politically consequential measure — suspending trade provisions under the EU-Israel Association Agreement — did not become the EU-wide action her speech suggested. Once again, it fell victim to capitals' reticence. The Quality Jobs Act is another delayed commitment. It was presented as a significant social-policy initiative, but the Commission is still putting out feelers and has not yet produced the promised legislative act. That makes it a one-year miss — but not an abandoned proposal. On migration, much of what von der Leyen promised last year involved implementing policies that were already under way, particularly the Migration Pact. However, one of the more identifiable new ideas — a dedicated sanctions regime targeting smugglers and traffickers — has yet to become the operational instrument the announcement suggested. And if migration remains one of the headline issues in her next speech, that will say something about how unfinished the agenda still is. Eliza Gkritsi contributed to this report. Advertisement

Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA View image in fullscreen Armed police at a checkpoint near RAF Fairford, Gloucestershire. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA UK news Suspect in RAF Fairford case called police to report incident Man dialled 999 before he and four others were arrested near military base in Gloucestershire, it has emerged Vikram Dodd and Helena Horton Tue 29 Sep 2026 17.35 EDT First published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 13.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford as part of a terror investigation that prompted fears of an Iran-backed plot called the police to report the incident, it has emerged. The call from the man, in his 20s and from London, was one reason armed police were scrambled to arrest the men, who were with three vans close to the military base used by the US in its attacks on Iran. The Guardian understands that police first on the scene found several barrels in the vans, one of which contained petrol, while the others were empty. An Iranian link to the increasingly bizarre events in the Gloucestershire countryside over the weekend is seen as increasingly likely, as the police and security services investigation continues. Senior US politicians, including President Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail. It was revealed on Sunday that a farmer driving home from a party at around 1am on Sunday had spotted the men and vans, and called 999. But why one of the suspects themselves called police is another strand of the complex investigation. News of the call to police by one of the suspects was first reported by the Times. A statement earlier from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons. Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.” The mounting view among investigators that Iran was involved was a key reason for Andy Burnham’s decision to call a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, which was attended by senior police and security officials. Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos. The suspects were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. The decision on Monday to bail the men came after examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London, all of which found no evidence of a viable device. Taylor said of the vans: “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered.” Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation, which is trying to establish why the five men, all British nationals from London, were in the Gloucestershire countryside, close to a sensitive site in the dead of night . The vans were marked by the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles. Taylor defended the decision to bail the suspects, saying: “Yesterday we released the five men on police bail. They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.” Residents were returning home on Tuesday after spending days evacuated from their village. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, claimed the events were the work of a “foreign actor” but did not provide further details. He said “a lot of people are disturbed” after the release of the suspects from custody. Trump had earlier said he was “surprised” the group had been freed. Speculation has been growing about a connection between the weekend’s incident and Iran. On Monday Taylor said he knew there was “significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident”. He added: “But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.” In March the British government gave the US permission to use the base for “specific defensive operations into Iran”. The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement. Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on the village of Whelford, where the men were arrested. Mark Richings, a butcher in Fairford, told the Press Association (PA): “There’s no change in here and we just got on with it as normal. We are a bit quieter today, but everybody seems to be OK, and we are having a bit of a chat about it. “We just carried on as normal. We have enough to do to occupy our minds. If anything did happen, there isn’t a lot we could have done about it.” Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels. Father Michael Robertson, the priest at the nearby St Thomas Catholic church, told PA: “A lot of parishioners didn’t think they could get to church. Those that came were worried but perfectly happy with the situation. “In fact, quite a lot of Americans who have deployed here actually come to mass and some of the permanently deployed Americans are full members of the parish. We’re quite contented with the situation generally.
